133-135, Water Jacket, Inlet Nut, & Inlet; 136, Water Pump; 137-140, Water Pump Shaft, Support Stud, Impeller, & Driver; 141, Water Pump Friction Sleeve; 142-143, Water Pump Friction Washer, Front & Rear; 144-145, Water Pump Bushing, Front & Rear; 146, Water Pump Gasket; 147-149, Water Pump Universal Joint Member, Male, Female, & Spring; 150-151, Water Pipe, Right Hand, Bottom, & Left Hand, Bottom; 152, Water Pipe Outlet Elbow; 153-156, Water Outlet Top Pipes for Cylinders.

**A VISIT TO THE FACTORY**

A visit to the Curtiss factory is of interest to any one interested in machinery and there you will see the latest machines of all types, from powerful milling machines to a delicate modern "Printograph" that is almost human in its manner of getting out letters and printing, for it is a cross between a printing press and a typewriter. Another unique machine is one that carves out propellers from a laminated block of wood. One arm of this machine runs over a model, and the other, about two feet away, arranged to move exactly with it, and provided with a tool of cutting edge, forms the propeller blade with absolute accuracy, out of a block of wood placed parallel to the model. The cutting tool follows all the complex changes in the surface of the wooden propeller with the greatest ease and rapidity.

The brazing room, where the oxy-hydrogen torch is used to braze metal parts together, and the room where they weld the water jackets on to the cylinders, are places of special interest; the nickel plating room, japanning room, and the room where painting and drying are done, almost complete the tour of the various departments, but there still remain the wood-working shop, boat shop, assembling rooms, where the aeroplanes are put together and completely set up, and the motor testing room, where motors are run for whole days, ten hours at a time, driving an air propeller and showing on scales the amount of thrust given at all times.

Here you may also see a machine to make "brake tests" of the motors, by which is told how much horse-power the motors give. This machine consists of a large drum with a brake fixed against it and cooled by water so it will not get too hot. This brake absorbs the energy of the motor, which is measured by an arrangement of scales and lever arms.

There is a tremendous racket when the big motors are running at full speed in this small room, and the hillside rings with the roar of their fiery exhaust.

In the laboratory of the factory, where the designs and drawings are made, there is one of the most interesting pieces of apparatus in the whole plant. This is a "wind tunnel," where models of aeroplanes are tested and where experiments are tried to see what occurs in the stream of air. Here tests are made which assist in determining what the best form and shape of objects such as upright posts and exposed parts shall be and where a measure of their relative resistances may be made. The tunnel itself consists of a square box with a propeller or fan mounted at one end to create a draft or current of air which passes through a screen to cause it to assume uniform motion. There is a window in the tunnel through which the observer can see the action of the objects to be tested. Varying the speed of the fan varies the speed of the air current and its pressure, and in this manner the stream-lines of air under the varying conditions and the effect upon models of different forms and shapes may be studied to enable refinements to be made in the aeroplane's construction.

Down on the shore of Lake Keuka, about a half mile from the factory, are the aeroplane sheds and the flying field. Here is where the aviation school is situated, and where flyers are made. Over the smooth field, the pupils start with the four-cylinder "grass cutters," or machines hobbled so they cannot get but a little way off the ground. They hop, hop, hop, almost all day long, one after the other taking regular turns, and now and again varying the monotony by being called away by the flying instructor to take a real flight in the hydroaeroplane out over the lake to get accustomed to the upper air, and to the high speed of the big machine.

Later in his course of instruction, the student takes out an eight-cylinder machine and flies around in circles over the field until he is able to take the test for his Aero Club of America License, which requires him to make two series of figure eights around two pylons fifteen hundred feet apart, landing each time within one hundred and fifty feet of a mark and rising to an altitude greater than two hundred feet.

This is the goal of the novice, and after his test, the student is ready to fly as far and as fast as he likes. He has become the complete airman.

John Andrew Riggs (1867–1936)
=============================

John Andrew Riggs was a pioneer, [politician](https://encyclopediaofarkansas.net/entries/Politics-and-Government-394), early [aviator](https://encyclopediaofarkansas.net/entries/Aviation-4589), patent medicine business proprietor, and father of [women’s suffrage](https://encyclopediaofarkansas.net/entries/womens-suffrage-movement-4252/) in Arkansas. Riggs’s Act 186 of 1917 allowed women to vote in the Democratic primary in Arkansas. This enfranchisement of women paved the way for Arkansas’s ratification of the Nineteenth Amendment to the U.S. Constitution.

John Riggs was born on November 5, 1867, in Shelby County, Illinois, the eldest of six children of Elbridge Marion Riggs and Sarah Ann Hubbartt. His parents were farmers and merchants. In 1877, the extended Riggs family moved to Sumner County, Kansas, the Southern border of which was Indian Territory.

In 1889, Riggs was one of over 50,000 pioneers in a line stretching for 100 miles along the southern Kansas border, waiting for the pistol shot that allowed them to vie for two million acres of claimable land. Riggs homesteaded 160 acres for fourteen dollars. He settled his land and, on June 29, 1890, he returned to Sumner County to marry Ida Louisa Callahan. They settled in Sheridan, Oklahoma.

For eleven years, Riggs raised cattle, farmed, traded, and served as a constable and [coroner](https://encyclopediaofarkansas.net/entries/office-of-the-county-coroner-14676/). His trading post was named Fence Post Johnnies’ for the lightning-proof fence post he invented to protect cattle from death due to lightning strikes. Riggs is recognized at the Oklahoma State Museum among 300 early Oklahoma pioneers whose names are embossed on a stretched buffalo skin.

In 1901, his wife and four children returned to Kansas. He sold everything and joined them in Wichita. Here, he developed the “Lopez Medicine Remedy” patent medicine. In 1905, he moved his family to Arkansas, launching Lopez Medical Remedy on Broad Street in downtown [Hot Springs (Garland County)](https://encyclopediaofarkansas.net/entries/hot-springs-887/). The medicine sold well nationwide until Riggs’s death in 1936.

In 1908, Riggs financed the Hot Springs Airship Company with local aviator Joel Rice as his partner. They incorporated and sold shares. In 1909, they took their American Eagle dirigible to New York City to the Hudson-Fulton Celebration week, participating in America’s first aeronautical show. One feature was their “Seeing-New-York-From-Above” vehicle that departed Madison Square Garden with fourteen passengers at a time and traveled over the city. “Hot Springs, Arkansas” was emblazoned on both sides. Meanwhile, the company built the largest steel-framed dirigible in America at Morris Park, New York, at a cost of over $5,000. After one trial run, a gale destroyed the facility, the ship, and the partnership with Rice. Riggs refused to finance a third dirigible unless he was given exclusive rights. A long, bitter lawsuit ensued between the parties in 1910 over the ownership of the company, which effectively ended the venture.

In July 1911, Riggs purchased the newspaper that would become the _Hot Springs New Era_, forming the Southern Newspapers company. He served as owner and publisher until he sold it to the Palmer chain in 1929.

Riggs was elected as a Democrat to the Arkansas House of Representatives, serving 1917–1919 and 1923–1925. Among his successful bills were those that mandated paving the Hot Springs to [Little Rock (Pulaski County)](https://encyclopediaofarkansas.net/entries/little-rock-970/)[highway](https://encyclopediaofarkansas.net/entries/roads-and-highways-4209/), established the city-manager form of government for Hot Springs, and passed a gross income state sales tax. He was also the author of the Primary Suffrage Bill, HB 340, which enfranchised women to vote in primary elections. HB 340 was a significant victory, making Arkansas the first non-suffrage state that allowed women to vote in Democratic primary elections. Introduced on February 7, 1917, the bill passed the House by a vote of 54–27, and on February 27, the Senate’s 17–15 “yea” vote gave full passage. Riggs was a Democratic candidate for governor in 1920 but was defeated in the primary by [Thomas Chipman McRae](https://encyclopediaofarkansas.net/entries/thomas-chipman-mcrae-114/).

Riggs died of cancer on March 4, 1936, and is buried in Hot Springs.

**For additional information:**“Air Age Comes to Spa Early; Airship Built Here in ‘08.” _The Sentinel Record_. April 27, 1958. p. 20.

HAMMONDSPORT. N. Y., June 7.-G.

H. Curtiess made two successful flights of

about two miles each here to-day with

the new aeroplane built for the Aeronaut-

ical Society. He described the figure eight

in his flights, and appeared to have the

machine under perfect control.

The new aeroplane will be entered in

the Morris Park competition in New York

next week.

Increase In Deaths for the Week.

An increase of 183 deaths in the city

last week, as compared with the corre-

sponding week a year ago, was shown in

the weekly report of Health Commission-

er Darlington yesterday. The total deaths

for the week ended Saturday was 1,405,

with a death rate per thousand of 16.06.

The diseases showing increases are

measles, diphtheria, heart disease, pneu-

monia, and tuberculosis. There was a

slight increase in the deaths of babies

with an increase of 53 in the deaths of

persons more than 65 years old. The in-

crease in the deaths of persons in tene-

ments was 147.

![Image 1: LIGHT AEROPLANE FOR MORRIS PARK; Glenn H. Curtiss's New Machine Will Arrive in New York This Week. EMBODIES MANY NEW IDEAS Weighs 550 Pounds and Has Lightest 25-Horse Power Motor Ever Built -- Trial Flights Successful.](https://s1.nyt.com/timesmachine/pages/1/1909/06/13/106719790_360W.png?quality=75&auto=webp&disable=upscale)

An event of unusual interest in New York's world of aeronautics will be the arrival this week at Morris Park of the new Curtiss aeroplane. The machine was ordered by the Aeronautic Society two months ago, and it was to have been delivered on June J, but Mr. Curtiss found it Impossible to finish the aeroplane by that time, and during the last ten days he has been trying it out in flights at Hammondsport. Its initial tests have been highly successful, the longest flight being one of two miles, making a number of difficult curves with the greatest ease. Mr. Curtiss will come down with the machine, and he proposes, to make some preliminary tests with it at Morris Park before the society gives its public exhibition, which will be either next Saturday or June 26.

The new machine is built on somewhat different lines from those formerly constructed at Hammondsport for Dr. Alexander Graham Bell's Aeronautic Experiment Society, of which the Silver Dart, now at Baddeck, N. S., was the most successful. In the main, it embodies the Curtiss aeroplane ideas, although it is the first product of the recently organized Herring-Curtiss Company. It does not, however, embody any of the methods toward securing automatic stability which Mr. Herring says he has successfully applied to the machine he has been building for the United States Government.

The conspicuous features that will at once attract attention from all students of aviation are the light weight of the machine, being but 550 pounds, making it the lightest successful aeroplane ever built, and the high horse power developed in respect to the weight of the motor. "We have been informed by good authority," said Mr. Curtiss last week, "that this motor develops more power per square inch of piston area than has ever before been obtained from a gasoline engine. I believe it is the lightest practical motor built. A similar engine of eight cylinders is now under construction."

The machine is a biplane, the surfaces having 20 feet spread and 4 feet deep from front to rear, with the same distances between. There are only 200 square feet of supporting surface. The framework is of Oregon spruce the carved ribs being laminated. The surfaces are made of Baldwin rubber, silk stretched to the tightness of a drumhead. A horizontal rudder containing 24 square feet is placed ten feet in front of the main plane, and a smaller adjustable horizontal rudder is placed ten feet in the rear. There is also a double front rudder, but either is ample, for vertical steering. The rear horizontal rudder also divides a vertical rudder of about the same area.

The machine, when on the ground, rests on three especially constructed rubber tired wheels, the front wheel being fitted with a brake to stop the machine quickly after landing. Stability is secured by movable surfaces at either extremity of the main planes. The operator sits in front of the radiator, behind which is the engine. The stability planes are operated by bending the body to the left or right as the machine heels over, through cables attached to a curved rod closely fitting around the shoulders of the aviator.

This engine is of the new Curtiss type, four cylinder, vertical, water cooled by force pump, 3 4 inch bore and 4 Inch stroke. The cylinders are cast iron with copper jackets homogeneously welded on. Lubrication is by a force-feed system, the pump being built in the case and operated from the cam shaft, the oil being fed through the hollow cam shaft to the main bearings and thence to the hollow crank shaft to the crank and connecting rod bearings, the overflow from the case returning to a separate reservoir underneath the engine, from which it is again pumped through the system. The crank case is of special aluminium alloy, and the shafts are of vanadium steel: The valves are both in the head and are actuated by single push rod and cam. All of the parts of the motor are made of special materials secured expressly for the engine. The weight, including the oil and water pumps, is 85 pounds. Ignition is obtained by Bosch magneto weighing 12½ pounds, driven by inclosed gears. The engine develops 25 horse power at 1,300 revolutions per minute, and has a maximum speed of 1,800 to 2,000 revolutions, at which it develops considerably more power. The engine is built for long and hard usage, the bearings are of liberal dimensions, and the lubrication and cooling systems are very complete. The motor has proved efficient in a ten-hour test. The single propeller in the rear, of aluminium, with a diameter of 6 feet. It gives a thrust of 25 pounds, though 150 pounds as proved sufficient to fly.

June 27, 1909

![Image 1: NEARLY A TRAGEDY AT AIRSHIP FLIGHTS; William H. Martin, in a "Glider" Towed by an Auto, Hurled Through a Fence. ONLY CUT AND BRUISED Glenn H. Curtiss's Aeroplane Makes Two Fine Straightaway Flights and Circles Morris Park Track.](https://s1.nyt.com/timesmachine/pages/1/1909/06/27/106720409_360W.png?quality=75&auto=webp&disable=upscale)

Marred by but one accident, which caused the hearts of thousands of spectators to jump up into their throats, the first public exhibition and tournament of the Aeronautic Society at Morris Park yesterday afternoon was pronounced by aeronauts one of the most successful events of the kind ever held in this country.

More than 5,000 people gathered at the track during the afternoon, and the scene in the grand stand reminded spectators of the old racing days, for not alone were the seats well filled, but the paddock and lawn were crowded with people. From 1 o'clock on until 8 the air was filled with flying apparatus of all kinds from the ordinary kite of the small boy to the aeroplane invented and operated by Glenn H. Curtiss.

There was to have been an airship contest, but the big dirigible balloon of the society was put out of commission in the storm of Friday evening, and it was impossible to repair it in time, so the event had to be postponed until next Saturday.

"Balloonatics" in the Air.

The first event on the programme was designated as a "balloonatics' obstacle race," in which the contestants were fastened to a light balloon and made to run and jump over obstacles while the balloon pitched and tossed them in the air. Those who took part in this event were George Bold, A. O. Danielson, J. M. Fisher, Dr. William Greene, A. E. Horn, George A. Lawrence, and J. C. B. Storrs. It was declared a draw.

Much interest was taken in the man-carrying kite of Israel Ludlow and in the towed flights of the gliders. Gliders are mammoth kites capable of lifting the weight of a man who is supposed to guide them while they are being pulled through the air at a rapid rate by an automobile. It was in the first of these events that the accident, which sent a thrill through the spectators, occurred. William H. Martin had taken his seat in the glider, at the south end of the track, and a high-powered automobile was hitched to the other end of the rope. Mr. Martin fixed himself securely in his machine and gave the word to go. The automobile started off slowly, but quickly got up speed, and by the time it had reached the grand stand was running forty miles an hour. There was a shout and a hurrah from the crowd, and then a sudden hush, as it was seen that something had happened that was not intended. The glider was seen to pitch and toss in the air from one side of the track to the other, and then it took a sudden dive into the fence. For a moment every one thought that Mr. Martin must surely have been killed, so swiftly was his glider going. It struck the ground and went entirely through the paling fence, smashing the machine completely to pieces. Mr. Martin lay still for a moment; then he crawled from under the wreckage, with only a few cuts and bruises to remind him of his narrow escape from death. The machine was wrecked and carried from the field in pieces.

Curtiss Machine a Real Flier.

The most sensational real flying of the afternoon was that of Glenn H. Curtiss, who made two straightaway flights and one circle of the track. Mr. Curtiss's machine was especially well tuned up, and he found the air conditions as near perfect as they should have been according to his ideas. He placed his aeroplane at the south end of the track and started his engines going. The propellers revolved with great rapidity and the machine shot ahead on its wheels for about 150 yards, when it rose gracefully in the air and moved on like a bird for 1,000 yards, when Mr. Curtiss brought it to the ground with perfect ease. Later on in the evening Mr. Curtiss accomplished something that he had never before attempted. He placed his machine in position at the north end of the track with the intention of making a complete circle of the grounds. Even his most optimistic friends who had watched his experiments doubted that he would be able to accomplish this, but he did it. He rose in the air 100 feet after his machine had started, and came down the home stretch at the rate of about 40 miles an hour like a boat on an even keel. When he reached the grand stand he commenced to turn, and by the time he reached the clubhouse he was half turned, and then he cut across the back field and upon the back stretch until he was within a hundred yards of his starting point, when he brought his machine to the ground, showing that he had it under perfect control.

Mr. Curtiss's machine, which was invented by himself, is a bi-plane. The surface have 20 feet spread, 4 feet from front to rear, with the same distance between. There are only 260 square feet of supporting surface, and the weight, including the aviator, is but 550 pounds. The framework is of Oregon spruce, and the surfaces are made of Baldwin rubber silk stretched to the tightness of a drumhead. There is a horizontal control surface containing 24 square feet, placed 10 feet in front of the main planes, and a smaller adjustable horizontal surface 10 feet in the rear. Stability is secured by movable surfaces at either extremity of the main planes, each surface being half within the main cell and half without. The operator sits just in front of the main planes, the radiator and engine being in his rear. The machine is controlled by means of a steering wheel placed directly in front of the aviator. Pushing out or pulling in the wheel steers the machine up or down. Turning the wheel right or left steers in the same directions.

There will be some real flying over the old Morris Park race track grounds this week. Glenn H. Curtiss's latest aeroplane, constructed for the Aeronautic Society tests of heavier-than-air machines, arrived on the Morris Park grounds early yesterday morning. The planes, rudders, and propellers were packed in a big oblong box, while in a smaller box was the four-cylinder motor, a veritable marvel in mechanical work for aerial flying, weighing but 100 pounds, and this includes the magneto, water pumps, and the oil supply. "I believe it is the lightest practical motor ever built," said Mr. Curtiss last week at Hammondsport, while trying out his latest creation, and experts who had the opportunity of inspecting it verified Mr. Curtiss's statement. It develops 25 horse power, and is water-cooled. S. Lynn Banter, who has general charge of the construction work in what is now the Herring-Curtiss factory at Hammondsport, N. Y., came down with the aerial outfit, and he will be joined by Mr. Curtiss to-day. Nothing was unpacked yesterday but the small box containing the motor, and only the cover of the box was removed. All that the curious members of the Aeronautic Society could see of their flying machine that possesses real possibilities was the tops of the four small compact cylinders. The neatness and general simplicity of the engine left a firm impression of its excellence upon the few students of aeroplane motor needs who took a critical peep at it.

“Looks good," said Wilbur R. Kimball, who was hard at work varnishing the planes of his big, eight-propeller aeroplane.

"The finest piece of motor work I have ever seen," was A. C. Triaca's comment, who made a brief visit to the workshop department in the society's grounds after a month's illness.

"We will hardly be ready to make even a trial flight before Tuesday afternoon," said Mr. Banter. "As soon as Mr. Curtiss arrives, the work of assembling the aeroplane will begin, and that will occupy the greater part of a day. Mr. Curtiss, I believe, intends to remain here a few days to give the machine a few trial flights before it appears in the society's public exhibition. He is particularly anxious to study the conditions for flying on the grounds. There is no question about the ability of the machine, as it has been thoroughly tested and has proved highly successful.”

Mr. Banter said that in all eight or nine flights had been made at Hammondsport during the last week, all but one being two miles or slightly more in duration. Although extremely light, weighing but 550 pounds, including the operator; Mr. Banter said he believed the aeroplane could carry two persons, but it is not likely that a passenger will be carried at present.

The arrival of the Curtiss machine seemed to impart additional enthusiasm in aeronautic work on the grounds yesterday, and despite the gloomy afternoon a number of members and their friends visited the place. Mr. Kimball said his biw aeroplane was all ready for, flight, and he expected to make an effort to rise in the air in the afternoon, but the rain prevented. His engine, which has not been working satisfactorily, has been put in perfect shape and all four cylinders are now working in harmony, whereas, in his previous attempts, only three cylinders would work. Fred Schneider's aeroplane has had a new motor attached, and he expects to be ready to rival the flights of the Curtiss machine within two or three days. Frank Rickman was on the grounds with several workmen, putting the finishing touches to his helicoptre, a curious and yet interesting looking contrivance, and several other machines were in various stages of completion under the big covered shed. There will be a lot of energy expended at the grounds this week, for every aero enthusiast who has a machine under way is determined to make a good showing in the coming aeronautic exhibit, which will be held either next Saturday or Saturday, June 26. The Directors of the Aeronautic Society will meet this week and formulate definite plans for the coming air flights. The Curtiss machine weighs 550 pounds, including the aviator. This is almost half the weight of the Silver Dart and of the Wright machines, being, up to the present time, the lightest successful aeroplane ever constructed in the world. Its two planes, as the machine is a bi-plane, are 29 feet wide and 4½ feet deep, with 260 square feet of supporting surface. It has horizontal rudders in front and rear, and both so arranged that they may be used for vertical steering. There is only one propeller, the blades, of aluminium, being 6 feet in diameter, and although it has a thrust of 225 pounds, the recent trial flights have shown that 150 pounds is sufficient for flying.

"MARTY” KEESE DYING.

City Hall Custodian Who Arrested "Boss" Tweed-Has Acute Bronchitis.

Martin J. Keese, janitor and custodian of the City Hall for nearly twenty-eight years, is dying in St. John's Hospital, Long Island City, of acute bronchitis. He has been in poor health for some time, and was taken from his rooms in the Hall to the hospital a week ago.

"Marty," as he has been known to Mayors, Aldermen, politicians, and newspaper men who have come and gone in the Hall for over a quarter of a century, has a most interesting history. He has been closely identified with all the important epochs of New York for fifty years. As a Deputy Sheriff he arrested "Boss” William M. Tweed at the old Metropolitan Hotel and Controller Connolly, and was the guardian of the latter during his incarceration in Ludlow Street Jail.

"Marty" was one of the organizers and leaders of the old "Vamps.” He is seventy two years old.

Take to the Skies
=================

###### PUBLISHED FEBRUARY 1, 2023 | WRITTEN BY EMILY COUGH | EDITED BY BHHS STAFF

![Image 5: Sepia photo of Alexander V. Wilson's motor-less plane with a few onlookers. ](https://barharborhistorical.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/09/323272354_946751863013649_3397103920504458328_n-scaled-1-1-1.jpg)

Welcome back to “Way Back Wednesday!” Last week we covered the sea with the “Queen of the Sea.” This week, we’ll take to the skies!

Extra! Extra! Read all about it! On October 17, 1908, The Evening Times of Pawtucket, RI, wrote an article about a man from Bangor who had built a motor-less airplane.

That man was Alexander V. Wilson, and he built the flying machine “in a bid to the government for a naval aeroplane.” The article goes on to state that this wasn’t the first machine Wilson had built, but rather just one of many.

In his efforts to test these machines, Wilson “had flown with them, most of his experiments having been on the ice in winter over Eagle Lake in Bar Harbor, and in summer along the shore.” In the article, he claimed in one of his previous tests, he was able to “[cover] seven miles and on another occasion rose to a height of 700 feet without the aid of a motor.” “Of course,” Wilson goes on to say, “[he] can only rise in the air and remain there without a motor provided there is sufficient wind.”

For an island that was only accessible by boat at the time, it must have been a sight to see for year-round residents if they saw Wilson testing his machines, especially if they’ve never been off island or seen a plane before!

Wilson took his invention to Morris Park in New York for an “aeronautic exhibition and contest,” along with many others, to compete for best in show. If you’d like to know more about the 1908 Morris Park contest, Tom D. Crouch’s article, “The Aeronautic Society of New York and the Birth of American Aviation, 1908—1918”, is an excellent read: [https://www.jstor.org/stable/23645508](https://l.facebook.com/l.php?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.jstor.org%2Fstable%2F23645508%3Ffbclid%3DIwAR2f8BudRPml77jvsGs26Wvl9Vy5Bs5Qf18GEUF9rS_PKkeDg8KmU7tfjwk&h=AT3vI0pQ7hlajKscEp2VmE6JhnDLQhV6O3NxKS_PyAFmzuCBTYM2iGeFq8IaUZD4o6MDh0haUn6TH09AzdsegM9kTHsGbK9KJHyHIIM2AKoZ1S3Sn7MS1-Rcyrbh2XNuY7SdA026yF7d-uQhh5YAnhOijQ&__tn__=-UK-R&c[0]=AT31Qp6QgiYs4Dp1nJ4T52pZpZ9WxSZ4ukz3yPk3umDX6PQGUSVNLrXAzsgttHn2rT4uVx7VoWZKT6Agmcd0-71gOtjphTbdrMxUfSZdBifMO4RUoFCNAOhy6SRIBP2l36r9Ny98h4iaRCxhx2_UbltHF4xOwfBqdtslReEa4cEqbYAvUomQWvWwh19z8gAMyGArknMU43ux)

While many of these names who competed in the contest, like Wilson, were nearly lost to aviation history, they were still a part of a time of great invention and innovation, to push the boundaries and laws of physics. They wanted to be a part of something great and new, just like the Wright brothers. And what an exciting time it must have been!

If you’d like to read the article in full and to read about the features of his plane, including “a movable fulcrum,” head to this link: [https://pawtucket.advantage-preservation.com/viewer/…](https://pawtucket.advantage-preservation.com/viewer/?k=wilson&t=33987&i=t&by=1908&bdd=1900&d=10161908-10171908&m=between&ord=k1&fn=evening_times_usa_rhode_island_pawtucket_19081017_english_11&df=1&dt=5&fbclid=IwAR1gnTvVUHbSaOCrZr00jRezgLtwyZjOrXyKggdGxoAH97EHlkXwC_8UoKc)

If you’d love to know more about Bar Harbor’s history and being a part of our legacy, consider becoming a member!

17.title: Aviation Biographies
17.content:
![Image 1: early aviator logo](https://www.aahs-online.org/images/misc/earlybird.png) HENRY W. WALDEN

Studied dentistry at Columbia University and, on graduation in 1906, opened a dental office in Manhattan.

In 1908 Walden joined the Aeronautical Society of New York, at the time based at the Morris Park racetrack in the Bronx. There he became interested in designing and building his own planes, the first two of which -- both biplanes -- were failures. For his third, he decided to try a different tack. To avoid long trips to Morris Park, he rented a loft near his dental office and, with the help of a cousin and a mechanic, began work on a monoplane.

During a test run on Dec 9, 1909, Walden’s fragile wood-and-fabric craft rose a few feet off the ground and traveled just over 10 yards before the plane’s one-gallon gas tank ran dry, becoming the first American monoplane to fly. However, this flight was discounted because of its brevity. So, on Aug 3, 1910, with a 10-gallon tank installed, he tried again and became airborne for a longer, albeit still brief, flight that ended in a crash, breaking several ribs and fracturing his collarbone. This epic flight made headlines in a NYC newspaper and the record book.

In late 1910, he teamed up with English flier George Dyott to established the Walden-Dyott Aeronautic Co at Hempstead Plains field to build monoplanes, but business was slow and, early in 1911, the two disbanded their company. Dyott received two of the monoplanes, which he later sold in South America, and Walden got the hangar and the unfinished third plane. Returning to his dental practice, he would put in a whole day there, then motorcycle out to the hangar to spend most of the night working on his planes, a grueling pace at best. In following years, Walden built nine more ships, performed at air shows, and survived at least a dozen more crashes.

In 1912, a flight student crashed in one of his planes and, while injuries were relatively minor, the accident so unnerved Walden that he quit flying to concentrate on laboratory work. There, in 1915, he invented and patented the first radio-controlled missile, a model of which is in the Smithsonian Institution. When the USA entered WW1, he formed a company with a New Jersey lumber mill to make aircraft wings and tails for the military. Then, in 1929, he formed Walden Aircraft at Long Island City; however, aviation had become a big business, and it was impossible for a small company to compete. In 1932, he sold his plant and went back to dentistry.

Walden died at age 81, one week before his induction into the National Aviation Hall of Fame 1964.

![Image 2: early aviator logo](https://www.aahs-online.org/images/misc/earlybird.png) Denotes an individual known to have soloed an aircraft prior to December 16, 1917, whether they were members of the "Early Birds of Aviation" Organization or not.

Archivist hopes Morris Park will honor its aviation history
===========================================================

By Ben Kochman Posted on [June 10, 2014](https://www.bxtimes.com/archivist-hopes-morris-park-will-honor-its-aviation-history/)

![Image 9: Archivist hopes Morris Park will honor its aviation history|Archivist hopes Morris Park will honor its aviation history|Archivist hopes Morris Park will honor its aviation history](https://www.bxtimes.com/wp-content/uploads/2014/06/21-airport-2014-05-22-bx01_z.jpg?quality=51&w=500)

Photo by Ben Kochman||

The old Morris park racetrack is famous – but how about some love for the Morris Park Aerodrome?

A local historian hopes his efforts to recognize his hometown’s unique aviation past will get off the ground.

Morris Park is well known for its namesake racetrack, which hosted the Belmont Stakes from the mid-19th century until 1904. But an archivist at Fordham Prep has tracked down evidence that the east Bronx neighborhood was once also home to some of the world’s first glimpses of flying machines.

**First helicopter flight**

“There’s very little of Morris Park history that we celebrate and put out on public display, “ said Louis DiGiorno, who came across his nabe’s aviation past while researching Fordham Prep alumni, many of whom were pilots. “With something this important, we should think about marking it.”

In 1908, the New York Aeronautical Society rented out the former Morris Park racetrack and invited some of the world’s aviation inventors – including the creator of the helicopter – to try out their flying machines at the site.

“Wilbur H. Kimbull’s heliocopter, upon which he has been working for several years, is being assembled at Morris Park and by the end of the week he expects to be ready to try the ascensional power of the machine,” read a story in the September 7, 1908 New York Times.

The airplanes that made it into the air did not go far. The show’s organizers removed the fences around the old racetrack to create an “unobstructed straightway for a flight of at least one kilometer,” according to the Times.

Trust us: Here’s a photo of The Aeronautic Society of New York testing its flying machines in Morris Park in 1908.

Some of the machines were able to take off — others just looked very impressive.

“The airplane that won design for best airplane couldn’t even fly,” said borough historian Lloyd Ultan.

**Proposed plaque**

The racetrack burned down a few years later, said Ultan, before the land was auctioned off in 1913 to residential real estate developers.

DiGiorno has proposed a plaque or flag in recognition of the area’s aviation history to Community Board 11.

He’s even got a neighborhood tagline ready:

“Morris park: looking up since 1908.”

Workers loading fuel aboard the Spirit of St. Louis on Long Island in 1927. That year, Charles A. Lindbergh flew the single-engine aircraft nonstop from New York to Paris, which kicked into high gear the idea of building a major airport in New York.Credit...Associated Press

*   Sept. 28, 2017

Q. I grew up in the northeast Bronx, and I remember my father and neighbors mentioning that back in the 1920s an airport was planned in the marsh. According to legend, a biplane came in for a landing and ended up in a cherry tree, destroying any chance of further developing the project. Is there any truth to this?

A. It’s true that a plane landing at the proposed site in 1927 crashed into a tree – although [it was an elm](http://query.nytimes.com/mem/archive/pdf?res=9D05E3DE143BE233A25750C0A96E9C946695D6CF). (No one was injured.)

That was a minor bit of turbulence, however, as plans for a major airport in the Bronx ran up against a much more difficult foe: the Great Depression.

Discussion of a large airport in the New York area dates to 1925, but little was done until 1927, when Charles Lindbergh’s solo trans-Atlantic flight kicked the effort into high gear. By the end of the year, the Commerce Department, led by future president Herbert Hoover, had identified six potential locations: four in New York City, two in New Jersey.

One of the New Jersey sites, in the Newark area, and now known as Newark Liberty International Airport, opened on Oct. 1, 1928. Plans for a New York counterpart would be complicated by a private company’s foray into the scramble.

That company was the Curtiss-Wright Corporation, at the time the nation’s largest aviation firm, which was formed in 1929 by the merger of several aeronautics companies.

MEADOWBROOK, L. I., Oct. 31.—With twenty-seven riders on the field and seventy-five fences to take in seven miles of continuous galloping, Meadowbrook members had the most successful drag hunt of the season this afternoon. The meet was at the Terrahau Farm, near Woodbury. The hounds caught the scent readily, and going toward Huntington they circled to Syosset. Those out included Acting Master of Hounds H. S. Page, Louis Neilson, James Parke, H. V. Bell, Mrs. Frederick Swift, H. Caswell, J. P. Grace, J. E. Cowdin. Malcolm Stevenson, J. S. Phipps. Harold Phipps, Devereaux Millburn, and Douglas Campbell.

In the morning those of the members who were sufficiently enthusiastic about the sport to get out before 9 o'clock gathered at Piping Rock Field with Ralph N. Ellis. A fox was soon started, after leaving the meeting place, but the high wind partly carried away the scent before the pack was well on the trail, and Reynard went to ground. Those out were Mr. and Mrs. R. N. Ellis, Mr. and Mrs. J. E. Davis, and H. H. Moore.

CANADIAN GLIDER IN TOWN.

Laurence Lesh to Give Exhibits at Morris Park on Election Day.

Laurence Jerome Lesh, a young man still in his teens, from Montreal, Canada, arrived in the city yesterday with a twenty-foot glider, which he will use in the aeronautic exhibition at the Morris Park race track on Tuesday. Lesh has been experimenting for some time in the art of flying, working out some new principles under the guidance of Octave Chanute, and he has made some very long flights in Canada. The glider that he has brought with him will be towed around the track by two automobiles connected with the glider by a long rope sufficient to enable the machine to reach a height of 100 feet. After sufficient speed has been attained the operator will cast off the rope and glide to the ground.

He will also exhibit a large box kite, which he proposes to launch from the top of the grand stand. Lesh will fly with the kite, and he says he can easily land in the field. Two or three other gliders will also be seen. Glenn H Curtiss's new aeroplane, which it had been hoped would be ready for a trial flight at Morris Park, is not yet ready for experimental work, it was ascertained during the week, and he will not be present. A number of captive balloons will be released.

Prof. A. J. Henry, the executive officer in charge of the Government Weather Bureau exhibitions, has sent a twelve-foot balloon, which is used for getting upper air records. A big hydrogen gas plant has been installed at the Morris Park aerodrome. The big kites to be shown are the same as used at the Research Observatory of the Weather Bureau at Mount Weather, Virigina, for taking the upper air temperatures and wind directions. The kites are about 5 feet wide and 6 feet 8 inches long.

The motorcycle championship races to be run on the track are well filled, and the star entries include Fred Huyck of Chicago, who holds many records; Walter Goerke of the National Athletic Club, Stanley Kellogg of Bridgeport, the 100-mile record holder, and A. G. Chappell of the New York Motorcycle Club.

BALLOON FOR MILWAUKEE.

Made in This City, and Major Hersey Will Make First Ascent This Week.

The new balloon which has just been completed in this city by A. Le Stevens for the Milwaukee Aero Club will be shipped to the club to-morrow, and late in the week the first ascension will be made. Frederick Pabst, the chief organizer of the club, and Major J. B. Hersey, who is in charge of the Government Weather Bureau at that place, will make the initial ascent with Mr. Stevens. The balloon will have a capacity of 62,000 feet, large enough to carry four passengers. The shipment of this balloon to the West indicates the increasing popularity of old-fashioned ballooning despite the fact that the leaders in aeronautics are disposed to frown upon mere ballooning as productive of little practical results. But it is a leader to other things, and the, unusual, interest in aeronautics this season in New England has been due primarily to the number of new clubs that have been organized since the first of the year and the many ascensions. Springfield, North Adams, Pittsfield, Hartford. Worcester, and Boston all have aero clubs, and there are prospects that a few more will be formed within the next few months. In the West ballooning as a sport has not been so active, although St. Louis, Chicago, and Canton have very flourishing clubs. A. Holland Forbes. who was one of America's representatives in the recent international balloon race in Berlin, has been invited to make an ascension with some of the army officers within the next few days at Fort Myer in the big Government balloon.

SOLDIERS' OLYMPIC MEET.

Attractive Programme Arranged for Twenty-second Regiment Games.

The Olympic meet of the Twenty-second Regiment Engineers on Nov. 25 will include a M. A. L. relay, 2,400 meters four-men team, open to the National Guard, United States Army and Navy. In addition, there will be a 4,700-meter (nearly three miles) invitation run. The Olympic and National, long-distance champions have been invited. The following athletes are expected to compete: Bonhag, Collins, and Joyce of the I. A. A. C.; Eisle and Bellairs, N. Y. A. C.; Riley, Mullen, and Malone of the Mohawk A. C.; Driscoll, Mercury A. C.; Carr of the Xavier A. A., Obermeyer of the N. A. C., and Spitzer of Yale University. This aggregation of athletes represents the fastest and best in America. The Twenty-second Regiment is the present military athletic champion of the United States, and has in its ranks some of the best athletic material connected with the Metropolitan Association of the A. A. U. There is a great deal of rivalry among the prospective competitors to win the point trophies, of which there are three—one for the most number of points of the meet, one for the relay, and another for the largest number of novice points. Considerable alterations are now being made in the armory to have everything in complete readiness for this important event.
